common_name: Kalinda Hens and Chicks (Skrocki Copper-to-Purple Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; a Skrocki-bred cultivar prized for its satiny leaves and shifting seasonal color.

directions: Bred by American Sempervivum hybridizer Ed Skrocki, 'Kalinda' forms a medium open rosette of satin-textured leaves that cycles through copper, olive, red, and purple tones across the growing season rather than holding one fixed color. New offsets travel out on unusually long stolons before rooting, so mature clumps develop a looser, more spread-out colony pattern than tight-clumping sempervivums. Grow in lean, mineral soil in full sun for the most saturated color shifts, and divide congested colonies in spring or fall.

common_name: Neptune Hens and Chicks (Skrocki Pink-to-Lavender Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this Skrocki hybrid is grown chiefly for its dramatic seasonal color turnover.

directions: Another Ed Skrocki introduction, 'Neptune' is a large, velvety-leaved rosette that runs through an unusually wide color arc over the year, opening pink in spring, fading to tawny yellow through summer, and settling into a soft lavender by winter. Its leaves stand more upright than the flatter rosettes typical of the genus, giving the clump a slightly domed profile. Plant in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun, where the seasonal color transitions show most clearly, and let mature hens set seed and die back naturally as chicks fill in around them.

common_name: Montfort Hens and Chicks (Van der Steen Cobwebbed Red Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; the fine webbing across the rosette is decorative but not a sign of pest trouble.

directions: Bred by Dutch hybridizer Van der Steen, 'Montfort' forms small, tight rosettes in shades of green flushing to red that are laced across the tips with fine, cobweb-like white filaments, a trait shared with the arachnoideum group of houseleeks. The webbing is heaviest in cool weather and on the youngest growth at the rosette center, thinning as leaves mature and expand. Grow in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; keep foliage relatively dry, since prolonged wet spells can mat the webbing and encourage rot at the crown.

common_name: Spherette Hens and Chicks (Skrocki Metallic Copper-Red Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun for the strongest metallic sheen.

directions: A Skrocki-bred selection, 'Spherette' forms an open, loosely cupped rosette with a distinctive metallic sheen, shifting between red and silvery green with coppery overtones depending on the season and light. Fine cilia line the leaf margins, catching dew and giving the edges a faintly bristled look under magnification. It is a modest, well-behaved clumper best suited to rock gardens, troughs, and crevice plantings where its unusual sheen can be viewed up close.

common_name: Lavender and Old Lace Hens and Chicks (Cobwebbed Heirloom Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; a long-established collector cultivar valued for its dusty lavender coloring.

directions: A long-cultivated hobbyist favorite, 'Lavender and Old Lace' bears medium rosettes in a dusty mauve-lavender that deepens with cold and sun exposure, edged with fine, lace-like cilia along the leaf margins that give the cultivar its name. The muted, antique color palette sets it apart from the brighter reds and greens common among modern hybrid sempervivums. It clumps readily from short-stemmed offsets and performs reliably in rock gardens, troughs, and green roof plantings, needing nothing more than lean soil and sharp drainage to thrive for decades.

common_name: Harry Mak Aeonium (Suncup, Variegated Miniature Aeonium)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in gritty succulent mix in partial sun; more commonly sold in the trade under the later synonym 'Suncup'.

directions: This variegated selection of the miniature species Aeonium castello-paivae forms densely branched, softly hairy stems bearing small rosettes only a few inches across, irregularly striped with cream or yellow against green and flushing pink at the margins in bright light. The finer scale and fuzzy stems distinguish it from the larger, smooth-stemmed variegated aeoniums already in cultivation. It goes semi-dormant in the heat of summer, needing water only sparingly during that rest period, and resumes active growth with cooler, shorter days.

common_name: Cornish Tribute Aeonium (Compact Red-and-Green Trewidden Hybrid)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in gritty succulent mix in full to part sun; tolerates coastal wind and salt spray better than most aeoniums.

directions: Raised at Trewidden Nursery in Cornwall, England, and a Plant of the Year finalist at the RHS Chelsea Flower Show, this compact, densely branching hybrid forms a low, many-stemmed mound of small rosettes with bright green centers surrounded by dark reddish outer leaves whose narrow tips curve inward. Its tight, clumping habit and small mature size make it far better suited to containers and small gardens than the tall single-stemmed species aeoniums. It shows unusually good tolerance of seaside wind and salt exposure, and holds its color best with strong light and lean, sharply drained soil.

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in gritty cactus-and-succulent mix in full sun for the strongest carunculation and blush color.

directions: Named in tribute to California hybridizer Dick Wright, this cultivar is grown chiefly for its carunculated leaves, thick and raised into small bumpy warts across the surface rather than smooth like most echeverias in cultivation. Leaf color runs from blue-green to grey with a heavy farina bloom, deepening toward pink or coral at the margins under bright light and cool temperatures. It forms a solitary to loosely offsetting rosette, propagating readily from leaf or stem cuttings, and should be watered deeply then left to dry out fully between waterings to avoid rot at the base of its textured leaves.

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in gritty succulent mix in full sun for the most intense pink blush and compact form.

directions: 'Blue Prince' forms a glaucous blue-green rosette heavily coated with powdery farina, flushing pink along the leaf edges when grown in strong, bright sun. Tall, wiry bloom stalks carry star-shaped red-to-pink flowers well above the foliage in the warmer months. It offsets readily around the base of the mother rosette, producing the dense clusters of 'chicks' that give this and related Echeveria hybrids their common nursery nickname, and it propagates easily from both stem offsets and individual leaves.

common_name: Big Wave Pig's Ear (Silver-Green Wavy-Margined Cotyledon)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings after callusing in fast-draining, mineral-heavy succulent mix; grow in full sun for the strongest red flush and waviest margins.

directions: 'Big Wave' is an upright, branching Cotyledon orbiculata selection with long, flattened, silvery-green leaves coated in protective farina and edged with a pronounced, undulating wave along the margins, a more exaggerated ruffle than the finely crimped edges of other pig's ear cultivars. Leaves flush red at the tips and edges under bright sun and stress. Pendant, bell-shaped orange-red flowers appear on tall stalks above the foliage in summer, and the plant tolerates being cut back hard to maintain a bushier shape as older stems become leggy.

common_name: Fuji Yuki Gasteria (Japanese Cream-Variegated Bicolor Hybrid)

planting.note: Pot offsets in gritty, well-drained succulent mix in bright indirect light; variegation reduces chlorophyll, so protect from harsh midday sun.

directions: Selected in Japan from Gasteria bicolor and named for the snow-capped peak of Mount Fuji, this variegated cultivar bears thick, tongue-shaped leaves striped in forest green, cream, and pink, with pearly white speckling scattered across the darker leaf portions. Color intensifies toward pink at the margins with more light, though full sun can scorch the cream-variegated tissue, so morning sun or bright shade suits it best. It stays compact and offsets steadily from the base, forming a tidy clump well suited to shallow pots, and tubular pink-and-green flowers appear on tall spikes mainly in winter and spring.
